pages.name: Off
pages.task: The gate is off, and 600 V sits across the switch. How much heat does it make?
pages.answer: Almost none, as almost no current flows
pages.why: Almost none. Heat is the voltage times the current. Off, only a tiny leakage current flows. So 600 V times almost nothing is almost nothing. The picture draws that leakage as zero.

pages.name: The hottest setting
pages.task: Which gate setting makes the switch hottest?
pages.why: Half on. There 300 V meets 10 A, which is 3000 W. Fully on, 20 A meets only 2 V. Fully off, 600 V meets almost no current. So half on is no safe middle. It is the hottest place to leave this switch. Held part on on purpose, with small signals, a transistor is an amplifier. That different job is taught in Instrumentation and control.

pages.name: What the sink can shed
pages.task: The junction may reach 150 °C. The air is at 40 °C. Each watt lifts the junction 0.5 °C. How much heat can this heat sink shed?
pages.why: About 220 W. The junction may rise 150 − 40 = 110 °C. Each watt lifts it 0.5 °C. So 110 ÷ 0.5 = 220 W. Fully on, 40 W is well inside that. Half on, 3000 W is more than thirteen times too much.

pages.task: You swap the IGBT for a MOSFET and leave it half on. What happens to the heat?
pages.why: It stays at about 3000 W. Half on, the switch still takes 300 V and passes 10 A. That is 300 × 10 = 3000 W, whatever the device. The gate drive changes what the control circuit must supply. It does not change the heat in the switch's main path.

pages.name: Twice the frequency
pages.task: You raise the frequency to 20 kHz. What do the edges make now?
pages.why: About 40 W. Each cycle costs about 2 mJ, 1 mJ an edge. At 20,000 cycles a second, that is 2 mJ × 20,000 = 40 W. The on part stays at 20 W. So the switch makes 60 W in all. The junction reaches 70 °C.

pages.name: No diode
pages.task: The switch opens on the coil with no diode. What voltage does the switch see?
pages.why: A spike far above 600 V. The switch tries to force the coil's current from 19.9 A to zero in about 0.5 µs. So di/dt is huge, and so is L di/dt. That voltage adds to the supply across the switch. It can break the switch down. With the diode, the switch sees only about 601 V.

pages.name: The coolest way
pages.task: You want the load to average 300 V from the 600 V supply. Which way keeps the IGBT coolest?
pages.answer: Flip it fully on and off, on half the time
pages.why: Flip it. At 10 kHz, it makes about 40 W: 20 W on and 20 W in its edges. Held half on, it makes 3000 W. The load averages about 300 V both ways. But the switch's heat differs by about 75 times.

pages.name: Nearly on
pages.task: The gate stands at 90%, nearly on. Can the 220 W heat sink cope?
pages.answer: No, the switch makes about 1080 W
pages.why: No. At 90%, the switch takes 60 V and passes 18 A. That is 60 × 18 = 1080 W. It is about five times what the heat sink can shed. Fully on, its voltage falls to about 2 V and the heat to 40 W.
